title: Hosting boundaries & keystore scan - intake with Asteria Health
summary: Intro discovery on hosting choices (hosted vs dedicated vs private) for HIPAA-sensitive EHR inference use case. Focus on key management/residency, audit/e-discovery, log retention & redaction, and fallback routing. SE to run short perf benchmark and ops checklist; security to receive SOC2 + keystore docs.
topics: HIPAA and GDPR overlap for patient data
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
Caching, KV cache, and PII leakage risks
next_steps: Marcus to schedule benchmark window (test dataset, 48h) - target 2026-06-25
Tara to send SOC2 report, private deployment playbook, and keystore whitepaper - by 2026-06-23
Customer to share minimal redaction rules and compliance checklist - Asteria Security - by 2026-06-24
action_items: Marcus Li - Provide benchmark plan and sample amp script - due 2026-06-25
Tara Nguyen - Email SOC2, ISO summary, and private deployment checklist - due 2026-06-23
Anjali Rao - Send list of required audit fields and legal hold needs - due 2026-06-24
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-06-21 14:00 PT | Duration: 47m | Attendees: Tara, Marcus, Priya (Redwood); Anjali, Ben, Karl, Lina (Asteria)

[00:00] Tara Nguyen: hey everyone thanks for joining — uh quick intros on our side, i'm tara nguyen account exec for redwood inference, with marcus li our solutions eng and priya in cs. how about you?
[00:08] Anjali Rao: hi i'm anjali head of security at asteria, we also have ben our clinical ml lead, karl cloud architect, and lina privacy counsel. we've been evaluating options for inference on PHI, so wanted to run through hosting and keystore boundaries.
[00:22] Marcus Li: great, yeah we're expecting questions around keystores, residency, and how logs are captured. just to set the stage — redwood supports hosted api, dedicated reserved pools, and a private control plane / on prem package. each has different tradeoffs for keys and logs.
[00:40] Karl Meyer: quick, uh, right away — our principal requirement is that patient identifiers never leave our purview. we need proof that the key material and primary audit logs remain in our region. can redwood keep KMS keys in our cloud account?
[00:52] Marcus Li: yes, so for private deployments we support customer-managed KMS/HSM where keys never leave customer boundary. for dedicated we offer bring-your-own-key for the control plane and optionally a customer-keystore in VPC; hosted api right now uses redwood-managed KMS but we do offer envelope encryption where you manage the root wrapping key — although that still results in some metadata held by redwood.
[01:16] Lina Park: that sounds like nuance we need to capture — is envelope wrapping enough for auditors? in past reviews we've been told only full key control meets our compliance posture.
[01:25] Tara Nguyen: understood. many healthcare customers treat hosted as acceptable only for de-identified pipelines. for PHI-backed inference we typically recommend private or dedicated with BYOK. we'll send our keystore whitepaper with options and control diagrams.
[01:38] Ben Ortiz: also curious about logging — we run e-discovery and legal hold; we can't have full transcripts stored in third-party blob for more than 30 days without specific controls. how are request/response logs retained and how granular are they?
[01:50] Marcus Li: logging gets split: control plane traces (per-request latency, routing) vs payload logs. by default hosted retains minimal logs for debugging and billing, but payloads are redacted. dedicated and private let you configure retention and export audit logs into your S3 or SIEM; private on-prem keeps everything in your environment.
[02:06] Anjali Rao: when you say redacted — is that automatic PII redaction or heuristic? we've seen automated redaction fail on clinical identifiers, and that risk is unacceptable.
[02:16] Marcus Li: fair point. redaction is heuristic in hosted — we try to remove clear PHI tokens, but we advise against relying solely on it. for dedicated/private we recommend pre-ingest redaction, tokenization, or client-side de-identification. we also provide hooks for prefix/KV cache controls so cached context can be segmented per-tenant and TTL'ed.
[02:36] Karl Meyer: explain this kv cache thing — our worry is that previous patient context could leak into future requests through the cache.
[02:44] Marcus Li: yes — so the runtime uses an LRU-backed KV cache for key-value activations; if you do multi-tenant or shared pools, we partition the cache by customer token and have strict namespace isolation. for private deployments you get physical isolation so no shared cache. there are also explicit cache flush APIs and per-request flags to bypass caching.
[03:05] Lina Park: and what about model fine-tuning or embeddings storage? we don't want derivative embeddings of PHI to be retained on vendor infrastructure.
[03:14] Tara Nguyen: embeddings and custom artifacts can be configured to stay in your VPC in the private offering. on hosted, embeddings are retained per our policy but can be disabled and deleted. we'll include the embeddings retention SLA in the doc pack.
[03:28] Ben Ortiz: latency vs cost — if we go private on-prem we might get better data controls but can we meet production latency for patient triage workflows?
[03:36] Marcus Li: depends on hardware. our dedicated pools are tuned for low tail latency; private on-prem depends on your infra. we can run a 48h perf benchmark using a simulated patient workload to measure p99 and throughput; that's what we propose next.
[03:50] Anjali Rao: okay please capture that benchmark scope in writing. also we need to evaluate fallback behavior. if the private instance can't handle a spike do requests fail open to hosted endpoints? that would be a compliance gap.
[04:02] Marcus Li: no, we don't fail open automatically. routing policies are configurable — you can set policy to reject, queue, or route to a dedicated fallback that is also within your tenancy. hosted fallback is opt-in and requires explicit agreement; we log every fallback decision in the audit trail.
[04:18] Lina Park: what about legal hold and exportability? auditors ask for a chain of custody that includes original request payloads and derivations. can you provide immutable logs with tamper evidence?
[04:28] Marcus Li: for private/dedicated we can export to your SIEM with signed logs and retention controls, plus an append-only storage pattern. for hosted we provide downloadable audit reports and signable summaries but not the same level of custody attestation unless under enterprise arrangement.
[04:44] Anjali Rao: we need SOC2 plus supply chain evidence. do you have SOC2 type II? can you share the report and pen test summaries?
[04:52] Tara Nguyen: yes we have SOC2 Type II and ISO scoping — i'll attach the report and an executive summary. mar- — sorry — and the security team can share redacted pen test results.
[05:02] Karl Meyer: small nit: network egress/residency. our EU sites require that logs and keys stay in eu-west-1. can you lock region-level resource placement?
[05:12] Marcus Li: yes, region pinning is supported. dedicated pools can be provisioned in specified regions and private installs are entirely under your control. we also have region-locking for keys and log sinks.
[05:22] Ben Ortiz: how do you handle consent/erasure requests under gdpr if a patient asks for deletion of their data that was used to prompt generation?
[05:31] Lina Park: yeah this is tricky because derivative outputs could be persisted in models or logs.
[05:36] Marcus Li: for non-training inference we don't update base models; derivative artifacts like embeddings or cached prompts can be deleted from storage upon request. for hosted customers we maintain deletion APIs and can scrub from backups per SLA, but we recommend private deployments when erasure guarantees are a strict requirement.
[05:54] Anjali Rao: need to confirm retention windows for backups and snaps — backups are often overlooked.
[06:00] Tara Nguyen: good point, i'll include backup retention details in the pack.
[06:04] Karl Meyer: any partner or competitor gotchas we should be aware of? we've looked at bedrock and the vendor ties to other models.
[06:12] Tara Nguyen: comp-wise, anthro- — sorry, anthropic and openAI give good quality but fewer ops controls. bedrock has region controls but is tied to the cloud provider's compliance flow. our differentiator is the unified runtime and explicit private install path with BYOK and audit export.
[06:29] Ben Ortiz: let's talk about the pilot — what does a minimal pilot look like? we want to run patient triage inference over de-identified records first, then a second pass with tokenization.
[06:40] Marcus Li: typical pilot: 2-week dedicated sandbox in your VPC or our dedicated pool with network peering, run a 48h perf window, run privacy tests (redaction effectiveness), and finalize keystore approach. deliverables: perf report, security config checklist, and integration notes.
[06:58] Anjali Rao: who owns the integration? we need an ops runbook for our SREs so they can rotate keys and trigger cache flushes on demand.
[07:07] Marcus Li: we'll produce an ops runbook and CI/CD snippets for key rotation, cache flush, and rollout steps. for private on-prem we can provide an install playbook and a support SLA.
[07:18] Lina Park: about KMS — you mentioned HSM options. are there FIPS-validated flows?
[07:24] Marcus Li: yes, when you bring your own HSM we support FIPS-backed keystores and HSM integration via standard KMIP or cloud KMS providers. documentation will show the flow diagrams.
[07:34] Karl Meyer: do you support split-key escrow or multi-party key management for escrow requirements?
[07:40] Marcus Li: we can integrate with third party escrow providers; split-key or multi-party is possible in private deployments but requires a slightly longer onboarding and legal arrangement.
[07:52] Ben Ortiz: any guidance on tokenization vs encryption vs redaction for PHI? our data science team wants embeddings from entire notes but we can't risk exposing identifiers.
[08:03] Marcus Li: recommended pattern: tokenization or irreversible hashing of direct identifiers before any external call; maintain mapping in your own vault. for embeddings you can produce embeddings on-premise and store them in your encrypted artifact store. if you need vendor-hosted embeddings, insist on private tenancy and strict retention + deletion policy.
[08:24] Anjali Rao: ok there are three compliance-check pillars — key residency, log custody, and deletion/erasure. if we can't get guarantees on all three, we won't move PHI to hosted.
[08:34] Tara Nguyen: that's standard — many customers start with de-identified hosted for early dev, then shift to dedicated/private for PHI. we'll run the bench and send docs to speed that evaluation.
[08:43] Karl Meyer: contacts for legal? Lina will need a data processing addendum and an updated security appendix.
[08:49] Tara Nguyen: i'll coordinate with our legal ops and add Lina to the thread.
[08:53] Ben Ortiz: small ops question — are model weights stored on the host or streamed? we worry about model snapshot persistence and snapshot logs.
[09:00] Marcus Li: model weights are managed by the runtime; for private you can host weights locally. we keep immutable model versions with digest hashes for reproducibility. we'll provide a model handling doc.
[09:12] Anjali Rao: ok, i'm also going to request architecture diagrams with call flows annotated for auditors.
[09:18] Tara Nguyen: absolutely, we'll include network diagrams, keystore flows, and log export examples.
[09:24] Karl Meyer: what about SSO and RBAC? we need SCIM and SAML with role separation.
[09:30] Marcus Li: supported. SAML/SSO, SCIM user provisioning, and fine-grained RBAC across model routes and billing tokens. in private you can integrate with your identity provider directly.
[09:41] Lina Park: do you have enrollment checklists for pen tests and regulatory questionnaires?
[09:46] Priya Raman: from CS we maintain a compliance onboarding checklist and we can run through it with you. we'll also hand over the standard questionnaire answers.
[09:54] Anjali Rao: great. one last thing — we need to understand cost implications; dedicated reserved pools look expensive but maybe better than a full private on-prem build.
[10:03] Tara Nguyen: yes reserved dedicated gives predictable unit cost vs variable hosted. private has capex and ops. as part of pilot we'll produce a cost projection comparing throughput and token economics.
[10:14] Ben Ortiz: ok let's recap actions.
[10:16] Tara Nguyen: recap: marcus will run the perf benchmark, i'll send SOC2+docs and legal contacts, anjali will provide retention/legal hold requirements, and we all rejoin after benchmark.
[10:26] Anjali Rao: sounds good. thanks everyone.

[End of transcript]
